circumlocution

sur-kum-loh-KYOO-shun · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Circumlocution is the use of many words where fewer would do, especially to avoid saying something directly; evasive, roundabout speech.

Instead of admitting he'd lost the report, he launched into a long circumlocution about 'temporary document displacement.'

Worked Example

When his mom asked if he'd finished his homework, Marco's circumlocution about 'still organizing his materials and reviewing the syllabus' was really just a long way of saying no.

Circumlocution isn't just wordiness -- it's wordiness used specifically to dodge a direct answer.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

evasion: Evasion is the act of dodging a direct answer by any means at all -- silence, a sudden joke, a change of subject. Circumlocution is one particular method of evasion: burying the point under so many roundabout words that the plain answer never has to be said.

wordiness: Wordiness is using more words than a message needs, and it is usually just careless or clumsy writing with no motive behind it. Circumlocution is wordiness with a job to do: the extra words are deployed deliberately to steer around something the speaker does not want to say.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

directness: plain, straightforward communication

conciseness: saying something clearly in few words

Where it sits · how far words wander around the point — vagueness → circumlocution → double-talk

vagueness vs. circumlocution: Vagueness is milder than circumlocution: it is simply being unclear, even in one short sentence, while circumlocution piles up whole detours of extra words to keep from landing on the point.

double-talk vs. circumlocution: Double-talk is harsher than circumlocution: circumlocution just wanders around a point with extra words, while double-talk is deliberately confusing language meant to deceive the listener.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — circum-

prefix — circum-: around (Latin)

root (rare, formal) — locution

root (rare, formal) — locution: a particular word, phrase, or style of speech -- locution is a real English word, just an uncommon, formal one (Latin loqui, 'to speak')

Put it together

Put it together: Circumlocution comes from Latin circum- ('around') + locution ('a way of speaking') -- literally 'speaking around' the point instead of straight at it.

Use the root in a new word: locution

Use the root in a new word: locution: Her old-fashioned locutions, like 'shall we away,' made her sound like a character from a costume drama.
